title: Finding the Pareto Frontier of Low-Precision Data Formats and MAC Architecture for LLM Inference
problem: Complex design space of low-precision data formats (integer, floating-point, posit, LNS) and MAC implementations (conventional and block-quantized) makes it difficult to identify optimal area/power/accuracy tradeoffs for LLM inference.
motivation: LLM inference demands efficient matrix multiplication; numerous data formats exist but their area/power/accuracy tradeoffs are unclear, requiring systematic design space exploration.
method: The researchers evaluated over 35,000 multiply-accumulate (MAC) circuits—the basic arithmetic components in neural networks—using six different number formats (INT, FP, posit, LNS, MX, VSQ) and various design parameters like operation size and accumulation width. Each design was tested for three qualities: chip area, power efficiency (measured in calculations per watt), and arithmetic accuracy (using signal-to-quantization noise ratio). The analysis then identified the Pareto frontier—the optimal designs where you can't improve one metric without worsening another.
key_novelty: The work comprehensively evaluates three relatively new number formats (LNS, MX, VSQ) for multiply-accumulate circuits used in LLM inference, showing which designs best balance performance, power consumption, and accuracy.
contributions: Systematic evaluation of 35,000+ MAC designs across multiple data formats
Pareto-optimal designs for INT, FP, posit, LNS, MX, and VSQ formats
1.8-2.2x TOPs/W improvement with LNS16/MXINT8/VSQINT4 vs. FP16/FP8/FP4
primary_theme: Pareto-optimal MAC designs for low-precision LLM inference
